## The program

```cpp
std::cout << "sum " << a + b << "\n";
std::cout << "difference " << a - b << "\n";
std::cout << "product " << a * b << "\n";

if (b != 0)
{
    std::cout << "quotient " << a / b << "\n";
    std::cout << "remainder " << a % b << "\n";
}
else
{
    std::cout << "quotient undefined\n";
    std::cout << "remainder undefined\n";
}
```

## Why the guard is not optional

A lot of languages raise an exception on division by zero, and the
habit that comes from them is to divide and handle the failure. C++
does not work that way: `a / 0` on integers is **undefined
behaviour**. The standard does not say it crashes; it says nothing
at all about what the program does from that point on. In practice
on x86 it traps and the process dies, on some other targets it
quietly produces a value, and with optimisation on, the compiler is
entitled to assume the division never happens and delete code around
it. None of those is something to rely on.

So the test comes first. `if (b != 0)` is not defensive clutter; it
is the part of the program that makes the division legal.

## Truncation, and the identity that decides it

```
 7 /  2 ==  3      7 %  2 ==  1
-7 /  2 == -3     -7 %  2 == -1
 7 / -2 == -3      7 % -2 ==  1
-7 / -2 ==  3     -7 % -2 == -1
```

Read the second column off the first with `(a / b) * b + (a % b) ==
a`. Since C++11 the quotient is specified to truncate towards zero,
so `-7 / 2` loses the .5 and becomes -3 rather than -4, and the
remainder is whatever is needed to make the identity hold — which
always gives it the sign of `a`.

Python chose the other consistent rule: it floors the quotient, so
`-7 // 2` is -4 and `-7 % 2` is 1, and its remainder takes the sign
of the divisor. Neither is wrong. They are different definitions,
and mixing them up is how an index computed with `%` ends up
negative in one language and not the other.

## The three lines that need no thought

Notice how much of this problem is just printing. `a + b`, `a - b`
and `a * b` cannot fail for inputs in this range, and writing them
first — before thinking about division at all — means the program
compiles and runs and prints something correct within a minute. That
is a habit worth having on much larger problems than this one.

## What this does not check

The cases all supply two readable integers. A real program would
have to decide what to do about `std::cin >> a` failing — a letter
where a number should be, or end of input. The reference returns
quietly in that case, which is enough here and is not a general
answer.
